title: Digging the Trench at Medina
text:
In 627 a coalition of the Quraysh of Mecca and their tribal allies, by far the largest army the Muslims had faced, marched on Medina. The Muslim community was small, and Medina had no walls.

According to the early biography of the Prophet by Ibn Ishaq, as edited by Ibn Hisham, it was Salman the Persian, a former Zoroastrian who had converted to Islam, who proposed a solution unknown to the Arabs: dig a trench across the open northern approach to the town, as was done in Persia. The rest of Medina was protected by lava fields, rocky ground and walled orchards.

Ibn Ishaq says the whole community dug, and that Muhammad himself worked alongside them, carrying earth. The diggers sang verses as they worked. When they struck a rock they could not break, they called the Prophet, who broke it. A later tradition says the emigrants from Mecca and the Medinans each claimed Salman as one of their own, until Muhammad said that Salman belonged to his own household.

When the confederate army arrived, its cavalry could not cross the trench. The siege dragged on for weeks. Supplies ran low, the allies distrusted each other, and a fierce cold wind battered their camp. In the end they broke up and went home. Medina was saved, and the Meccans never again attacked the town.
lesson: A good idea can come from the newest member of a team. It works best when everyone, including the leader, takes up the shovel together.
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Life of the Messenger of God), as edited by Ibn Hisham; translated by A. Guillaume (1955)
caveat: The details come from biographical traditions written down more than a century after the events.
